books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Table of United States territorial acquisitions; areas and prices from the historical record. See Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 7.
stimulus.text:
| Acquisition | Year | Area | Price |
| Louisiana Purchase | 1803 | 827,987 sq mi | $15 million |
| Florida | 1819 | 72,101 sq mi | $5 million in assumed claims |
| Texas annexation | 1845 | 389,166 sq mi | Annexation |
| Oregon Treaty | 1846 | 286,541 sq mi | Treaty |
| Mexican Cession | 1848 | 529,189 sq mi | $15 million plus $3.25 million in assumed claims |
| Gadsden Purchase | 1853 | 29,670 sq mi | $10 million |

source: original; stimulus is a table of United States territorial acquisitions compiled from the historical record
stem: According to the table, which acquisition cost the United States $10 million?

options.misconception: The Louisiana Purchase cost $15 million in 1803.
Florida cost $5 million in assumed claims in 1819.
The Mexican Cession cost $15 million plus $3.25 million in assumed claims.

rationales.B: Florida cost $5 million in assumed claims, not $10 million.
rationales.C: The Gadsden Purchase row shows $10 million for 29,670 square miles in 1853.
rationales.D: The Mexican Cession cost $15 million plus $3.25 million in assumed claims, not $10 million.
rationales.general:
1. Run down the price column. Louisiana $15 million, Florida $5 million, Texas annexation, Oregon treaty, Mexico $15 million.
2. Find $10 million. It sits in the last row, the Gadsden Purchase of 1853.
3. Note the size. At 29,670 square miles, it was the smallest addition in the table — and the last.
Remember: when a question asks for a number, read the column, not the story. The price column answers it in one line.
